div.head: EASTERN AFFAIRS.
div.p: EASTERN AFFAIRS.

' News of the war in the East of Europe, the late armistice and its duration, and the terms of peace which are likely to obtain the approval of the Powers and of the Turkish Government--these and the still widening nud deepening expression of public opinion, individual and collective, in England, con- ktitute the one absorbing topic of interest, not merely in Great Britain, but throughout the whole of Europe and the civilised world. We can only indicate some of the leading points of interest which, during the last few days, have become specially prominent.. Respecting the conditions of peace, " The Nord of Friday published a telegram from Constantinople, dated September 23, stating that the following are the points pro- posed by England to Servia as the basis of the uegotiations for peace :- 1. An unconditional armistice. 2. The status quo ante bellum to be main- tained for Servia and Montenegro, with an extension of territory for the latter. 3. A liberal ocal autonomy for Bosnia, the P erzegovina, and Bulgaria. The adhesion of liussia, Germany. France, and Italy to these propositions is stated in the telegr,iin to be certain. 1 he armistice between Turkey and Servia which was to have terminated on Modday, has been pr longed for eigh days. in agreeing to this colL se, the Porte expresses a hope that the Powers, during the extended cessation of hostilities, will communicate the Conditions of peace they propose. A Berlin telegram to the Pall Mall Gazette states that all the Powers have agreed to accept the English peace proposals, but according to a Reuter's telegram from Pesth Austria has no yet adhered to the conditions.

The Rev. G. S. Reaney, late of Wycliffe Church, Warriniton, but now in charge of a congregation at Reading, took part a few days since in a public meeting, held in that town, convened to denounee the Bulgarian atrocities. Many of our readers will be glad to learn the opinions of a gentleman who, in times past, has taken a prominent _part in public affairs of Warrington and the district.

The Rev. G. S. Ricanrav moved the following reso- lution :—" That this meeting is of opinion that prompt and energetic measures should be taken by her Majesty's Govertment, in conjunction with the other European Powers for preventing a repetition of the atrocities, and for bringing to puieshment the princi- pal actors therein, and also for demanding such repara- tion as may be possible for the injuries whieh have been inflicted upon the Bulgarians; and this meeting is also of opinion that an intimation should be made to the Turkish Government that the support of Eng- and will not be continued to Turkey unless its Go- vernment will do the best in its power to inflict such punishment and make such reparation." The rev. gentleman prefaced his remarks by apologising for oc- cupying such a prominent position in the meeting, having, he remarked, only recently taken up his resi dense in the town. He had been led to suggest the meeting by a letter to the newspapers, as he thought there was a little hesitation in some quarter where there might have been energetic action. (Hear.) He considered a meeting like this, when they took all the circumstances into consideration, was one of great signification. All classes throughout the country were being deeply moved on the subject they had met to consider, perhaps it might be to some extent ley the we nf exaggerated words; but there were times when m to had better deal with exaggerated language than w.th coldness of heart. (Cheers.) He had read in that day's papers the speech of a gentleman (referring to Mr. Fremantle, the Conservative candidate for Bucks) who thought the question of local taxation, at least to agriculturists, was of more importance than the Bulgarian massacres, (Voices : " Oh, oh.") He (Mr. Heaney) differed from Mr. Bourke when he said they were not met there to dictate to the Government. He liked to think that the people of England are greater than any Government. (Hear and cheers.) He had been trained not to caet his responsibility upon any political party, and felt that they should meet there, if not to dictate to the Government, nor in any antag- onism to them, at least in some measure to correot their policy. His resolution concerned the immediate fature, and on it they asked the Government to act. They had heard something about these atrocities, and he was of opinion that that part of any mates speech which was silent was the moat eloquent in regard to them, for there were things which a man could hardly speak about. He understood from the newspaper ac- counts, and from things which he had been told, that we in England could not realise to anything like a full degree the enormous wickedness which had been per- petrated in Bulgaria; and what they wanted to do was to feel that this was not altogether an isolated episode in Turkish history. Many of them would remember the events that happened in 1858, and what was done In Syria in 1860—things which, but for the intervention of Preece, might have grown into the proportions of the Bulgarian atrocities. [hese were not the " inci- dents of war," but the incidents of Turkish misrule, and the sooner they realised this the sooner they would rise to their duty. (Hear.) His resolution demanded that justice should be done to the chief so ors in these atrocities. He felt that all would agree with that, (Hear.) He thought the voice of England was the voice of justice when it asked that the chi f actors ehould he punished on the spot where the barbarities were committed. (Cheers.) The re- solution further asked that relief &mid be given—he thought provided out of the freasury of the I urkish Governm nt— (hear, hear)—to those of the Bulgarian, who remaieed alive; that their houses should be re- built and their cattle restored to them, as had been done for the Turkish h If of a village which had been burnt by the Bulgarians. (Hear.) then it also asked that these Christian provinces should not be handed over again to the rule of the Turks. (Hear.) He knew it was said by those gentlemen, the hangers-on at the London clubs, and the quasi-official world, "Cannot a Turk do what he likes with his own ? " But that which he took with such utter and monstrous cruelty was not his own. It was not his to destroy the house, to rob the furniture of church and school, and owrage the Wives and children of peaceable subjects. (Hear.) MANCHIEBTEB, Bartransr.—The improved tone reported last week has been tolerably well sustained during the present. Business has been fairly active, and prices well sustained in their firmness, with a slight advance gained in a few instances. The bulk of the business concluded has been in articles mast in request abroad and directly for export. Manufacturers, as a rule, axe fully em- ployed; in many cases they have as much on their books as they can conveniently execute within the next few weeks' still, considering the period of the year, it cannot be doubted that the volume of business is below the average. The home demand increases but slowly, capital remains locked up, and capitalists will not speculate.

At the Altrincham Petty Sessions, cu hlonday, the overseers of the different townships in the Petty Ses- sional division of Altrincham submitted to the b ouch printed lists of the persons liable to serve on juries for verification and allowance. The bench suggested that in future the overseers should submit them before they were printed to the nearest magistrate, so that they might see whether there were any omissions or mistakes which required rectification. CHESHIRE MYSTERY. (From the ,Alancicestcr Guardian.)

We are constantly reminded that the world is, after all, a small place, and that we never know where acquaintances may turn up. The readers of the Eng- lish journals heard a few days ago of a French tourist, one M. de Tourville, who lay under suspicion of having been accessory to the violent death of Madame de Tourville somewhere in the Tyrol. He had gone out for a walk with his wife, who was said to be a lady of Eaglish birth, and had returned alone, saying that she had been seized with a sudden fit of giddiness and had fallen down a precipice, which statement speedily obtained such confirmation as could be derived from the finding of her mangled body at the foot of a lofty rock. The Austriau police thought it necessary to arrest the husband and institute an inquiry, but no cir- cumstances flatly contradictory of his account of the tragedy o uld be discovered, and, he was set at liberty. rhis story connects itself with an event the occurrence of which iu the neighbourhood of Manchester created a vivid but brief sensation a little more than eight years ago. The event was the death of Mrs. Brigham, of Foxley Hall, near Lymna through the accide ital discharge of a revolver in the ha.uie of her son-in-law, a Frenchman. M. Perreau, as he was then called, had been very recently mairted to Mrs. Brigham's daughter, a young lady of infirm health, and w e be. lieved to be iik ly topcoat largely by the misadventure in which he had nad so unfortunate a part. Our columns of the date contained a brief lichee of the in- quest, which resulted •in a verdict of .4 accidental death," coupled with a reproof of the Carelessness of Which M. Perreau had been guilty. If it be true, as is now stated, that M. Perreau subsequently took the name of Be Tourville and that he is the person who lost his wife in the Tyrol a week or two ago, it will be admittted that he has been the subject ot a singular succession of fatalities. It should be observed that according to the accounts before us the Madame de Tourville who perished on a lonely mountain side was not the lady from Cheshire—who died, indeed, about two years after her marriage—but a second wife, who is said to have brought to her hmband a fortune of £70,000 and to have disposed. of it by will in his favour. The facts when compared with the most startling plots of OUT modern novelists wit show that panting art toils in vain to keep up with veracious history. We re- gret to add that, as M. de Tourville or Perreau had been discharged from custody, nobody alpears to be keep- ing an eye on the future course of his remarkable ; fortunes.

The fortnightly meeting of this authority was held on Tuesday, at the Runcorn Workhouse, under the presidency of the Rev. Canon Barclay. According to instructions from the board, Mr. H. Bancroft, C.E., Manchester, presented a report on the scheme for sewering that portion of the township of Appleton comprising Wilderspool and Stockton Heath. At present there are no main sewers in either of the two latter places, the existing shallow drains, discharging themselves into ditches by the roadsides, where the water becomes stagnant, offensive, and injurious to health. Mr. Bancroft proposes to put down sewers, concentrate them to one outfall, and filter them through tanks by means of lateral filtration, the Effluent water from the filters to be run into the Lumb brook near its junction with the Mersey. The estima- ted cost, exclusive of purchase of land and way -leave, is £3511. A committee, consisting of Sir Gilbert Greenall, Thomas Lyon, Esq., the chairman, and Messrs. Knowles, Baxter, Weir, and Dodd, was ap- pointed to consider the scheme.

div.p: TURKISH Al ROCIMS IN BULGARIA.
MEETING AT LYMM.

On Tuesday evening a large and enthusiastic meet- ing wus held at the Congregational Schoolroom, Lymm, to protest against the Bulgarian atrocities. Mr. 3. Barton, J.P., presided, and on the platform were—Mr. ylands, ALP., Rev. W. D. Fox, Rev. Mr. Bun, Mr. Dutton, chairman qi the Lymm Local Board, Mr. Brown, Mr. Thomason, Mr. Davies, and other gentlemen.

The Cavil:KAN read a letter of apology for inability to attend from Mr. T. Y. Ridgway, solicitor, and ex- pressing sympathy with the objects of the meeting. The following letter was also read : Statham Lodge, Warrington, September 26th, 1876 My Dear Mr. Barton —I find that lam not able to be present at the "Bulgarian Atrocities" meeting this evening, and there to support the chair, as I should mach like to have done. I am, at the same time, not quite sure that I should have been on the aide of the majority. If the meeting is intended to assist the Bulgarians out of the grievous difficulties with which they are now beset, it has my cordial sympathy; but if it is intended also to censure the British Govern- ment, I think that the effect of it must be either mis- chievous, or, at best, useless. The Government are alone responsible to the nation and to Europe for the good conduct of their negotiations with Turkey and the other Powers affected. And it is self-evideet that, during tho existence of diplomatic difficulties, our own or any other Government must find it impossible that they should take the world into their confidence, and proclaim exactly what are the obstacles in their way. It may be all very well for party objects to censure the unknown acts of a Government, but we must all bear in mind that the doing so at this moment may mislead entirely, and I believe has already seriously misled Continental nations, who are generally incap- able of estimating at their correct value opposition speeches here, and that a very slight mistake may bring about a greater war than the one we have now to deplore. With 81 ton guns, I fear that war, when it does come, must be at least as atrocious as any that the world has hitherto known.—Yours very truly, PETER STIIB3. John Barton, Esq., Chairman "Bulgarian Atrocities" meeting. The CitAIIIMAN said from physical inability he would not address the meeting, but at once call on The Rev. D. Fox, rector of the second madiety of Lymm, to move the first resolution, which was as follows ;—" That this meeting has heard with indite., nation of the atrocities perpetrated by the Turks upon - the unarmed population of Bulgaria, and earnestly and respectfully urges her Majesty's Government to take., such steps as may best contribute to render the recur- rence of similar atrocities impossible." The rev. gentle-, man said some of the chief atrocities which had oc- curred had taken place in a village school room, there- fare it was fitting that the villages as well as the large towns of England should speak out upon this great que,tion. (Cheers.) They had seen enough to stir the sympathy of every feeling heart, for the more the evi. deuce of these atrocities increased the worse the actual staet of affairs seemed to be. It was the habit of some parties in the House of Commons to diminish as far as possible the accounts that reach the ears of the public, and it was said that the atrocities were not nearly so bad as they were represented, and that the cruelties were equally bad on both sides. It was the policy of the Government to withhold from the nation whatever information they had, and it would seem that the Government were aztually in a state of ignor- ance as to the actual state of affairs. Notwithatanling the fact that we had a large consular force in Turkey, and a well manned embassy, the correspondents of the daily newspapers were actually in possession of the facts of the case before the representatives of Great Britain were. (Shame.') We had not only that remark. able report of the United States Consul, but also Mr. Baring 'e report, which confirmed the story of the atro- eitiee, and not only so, but the respon-ibility of the Turkish G wernment was most clearly brouzht out. ("Shame ") In three or four instanms the leaders of these barbarous outrages had received decoration and promotion from the hands of the Turk.sh Government. We had been asked to place implicit confidence in the Government of this nation, but we were not prepared to do that after:the reticence which"they had exhibited. The nation had shown an extraordinary amount of patience in waiting 30 long for the information. and in trusting to their representatives to do the best they possibly could, and it was surely a most absurd thing when a nation had expressed its opinion upon their conduct in an unmistakeable way, that we ehould be told to calmly trust to a certain Power above us, and I believe that one whon we know from hissewn lips to be on the aide of the angels, would do all things for the best. (Laughter and cheers.) Never had we had such an instance of more extraordinary affrontety than the way in which it was taken for granted that the English nation ought to trust the whole of the issue of these events to one or two individuals who were known in feeling and opinion to be entirely con- ' trary to the expressed opinion of the nation. (Loud cheers.) He hoped that immediate steps would be taken to prevent a recurrence of these abominable atrocities, (Cheers.) He concluded by moving the resolution, and sat down amid great applause. Mr. RYLANDS. M.P., on rising to second the resolu- tion was received with loud and prolonged cheering. He said he came there as a neighbour, and not as a stranger. (Hear, hear.) He had been invited to take part in meetings in other parts of the country, but he hid thought it desirable to refuse the invitations be • cause he had been anxious that this great spontaneous expression of public feeling against these abominable atrocities, should not be open to the suspicion that it was the work of any agitation or movement outside the respective localities in which the meetings were held. (Hear, hear.) He had always said it was exceEd • ingly desitable that the inhabitants of the plO5 should be those to stand on the platform and give voice, to the feeling of the locality, in order that the Government might understand that this was almost the unanimous feeling of the people of this kingdom. (Cheers.) He understood that this meeting was not of a party character, and. that it was for all parties to unite together In one expression of opinion on this subject. (Hear, boar.) He mould quite understand that it was right that there should be a meeting in which all classes of opinion should be represented This great evil against which protests were being made, was the remelt of the traditional foreign dace policy, which for many years past and under different Governments, had led the influence of thie country to be given in support of Turkey in all its abomination , out of fear lest some danger should arise from the aggression of Russia. It was in cousequence of that feeling we had the Crimean war. He had been charged by a certain portion of the daily press that in his speech at Warrington, he did not tell the people that the Crimean war was the work of a Liberal Govern- ment. He had not mentioned it because he thought everybody was aware of the fact that it was Lord Palmerston's Government which had commenced that war. In that Government many Liberal statesmen, such as Lord Russell, Mr. Gladstone, the Duke of Argyll, supported the Crimean war, and unfortunately the people of this country, and the great mass of the Liberal party, went with the Liberal Government in support of that wicked war. However, there was a small section of that party, including Cobden and Briglat—(oheers)—to which he also belonged, that pro- tested against the policy which was then pursued • That section charged their own Government with being traitors to the best interests of the country, and with having committed a great political blunder. Therefore he felt he had a perfect right to appear on that platform, and condemn the polioy of the present Government with perfect freedom. (Cheers,) He did it against his own party when they made the same mistake, and he would certainly not withhold his voice when the Coneervative Government were purbuing a similar counts. (Cheers.) He was prepared to say that the Gevernment of this country in cerrying out the old traditional policy of the Foreign Office, were ear. ry ins out a polio' which, if continued. would mid in disaster and injury. (Rear, hear.) Because one statesman had been wrong and adopted a wrong policy, that was DO reason why it should be reveries. • West pursued. New circumstances and events arose which made it wise to change that policy, and we had the eminent men whom he hod named, and Lord Strat- ford de Radcliffe, changing their policy of former years. It seemed to him that the Conservatives were no more bound up by this Foreign Office tradition than the Liberals were. (Hear, hear.) There Was a large number of CODS arvatives throughoat the country who were protesting against the policy of the present Government. In the House of Commons some mem- bers, even before Parliament separated, rose from the Conservative benches and expressed a very strong opinion in favour of justice being done to the Christian provinces who were struggling for freedom. Honour- able friends of his own, Conservative members of dis- tinction, Sir Henry D. Wolf and Mr. Forsyth, who they were familiar with Eastern allairs,advocated considered, and what he consi lered, to be a more en- lightened policy on the part Of the British Govern- ment. A very large number of Conservatives were seriously dissatisfied with the policy which had been pursued, and he found that morning that it was re- ported that a round robin had been signedley 80 Con- servative members expressing their dissatisfaction with Lord Beaconsfield's speech, and asking the Govern. meat to call an autumn session, in order that the ques- tion might be discussed and public opinion brought to bear on the Government. (Cheers.) He had also read that in the Cabinet itself there were rumours of differences of opinion, and that certain members of the Cabinet took a different view of the matter f rein Lord Derby and Lord Beaconsfield. Pos- sibly these reports were untrue, and he was not going to say that they were authentic. But if they were untrue now it was very likely they would be true before long. (Cheers.) They were coming events which cast their snadows before. (Hear, hear.) He had not that low opinion of the great majority of his Conservative fellow countrymen, amongst whom there were many patriotic men of high sentiments, that they would fail to express an opinion such oB would compel the Government of this country to alter their policy. Possibly some members of the Cabinet would not submit to it, and there would ensue a recon- struction of the Conservative Government, and they r Would have a Government that would obey the strongly expretsed will Of. They did not want, to raise a party issue, what he wanted was to comps' the Conservative Government to do that which he be- lieved to be rig, t. as he thought they were the mee best able to deal with the difficulty. If they would accept the expression of public opinion which had been so general throughout the country, he had no hesitation in saying that a eewly constructed Censer- vative Government would be able to sati,fy the just expectations of the people. (Cheers.) The barbarity of the Turkish nation was no new thieg. For four centuries the career of the Turkish Government had been one cohtinuel source of eborninale crimes, even worse than those, the intelligence of which had just reached England by means of the penny press. To show that this was no new thing he would give them a single instance vrech occurred in 1822, not much more than fifty years ago. In consequence of the Turkish Government oppressing the Christian population in the Grecian Islends, one of the islands, Scio, rose in revolt. It was a beautiful islend, one of the most prosperous in those seas. It was inhabited by an indus- trious, prosperous, and happy Christian p,puktion, and in cons quence of the horrible barbarities of the Turkish soldiers the population, which in the begin- ning of the year was 120 000, was reduced at the end of July t.) 900 persons. (Seetne.) Amongst the prisoner were 700 persons, whom they meant to divide as slaves, but they were brutally murdered because their captors , quarrelled over the spoil, and 95 Greek merchants who I had been taken as hostages and delivered up in good faith were cruelly put to death. The industry of the Christians had always been robbed by the Turkish oppressor in every part of his dominions. Christians had common justice denied them, and they were not allowed to wear arms and they were subject to any crime which the Mussalmen might choose to perpetrate without getting reparation. Their lives and the honour of their women had been at all times unsafe, and those people who had aspirations and desires to progress, were held down by the vile hand of the Turk that crushed them to the earth, and robbed them of those blessings which God in hie providence in- tended them to enjoy. (Shame.) That had been the ' universal character of the Turk, and that was the manner in which the peasants of Herzegovina had been treated. He had no hesitation in saying that if there ever was an insurrection that was justifiable and honourable, it was the rising of the Herzegovinians against this despotism which was crushing their liberty. (Cheers.) He had seen from the correspon- dence in the Blue Books, a long statement a the grievances- of these poor people, and which had been laid before Government. In the most piteous manner they implored the powers of Europe to do something to relieve them from this dreadful condition' all they wanted was for the hand of the Turk to betaken off them. They even offered to be placed under a Govern- ment, and under a prince appointed by the Powers, who should not be a native Herzegovinian, offered in fact to do anything provided they might have their life and liberty, and be relieved from Turkish oppression. They said they were determined not to live under such abominable misrule any longer, and if the Powers would n3t help them, then they would fight for their liberty. He could easily imagine the feelings of the country from which such letters and piteous appeals proceeded, but Lord Derby turned a deaf ear to every , consideration of humanity. (Shame.) This appeal ' Lord Derby received without manifesting the slightest sympathy. (Shame.) He was speaking from the authority of the Blueßooks,extracts from which he had, copied that day. Lord Derby took two courses when he found these poor people were rising in insurrection, One was to say to the Turks " Take instant measures, the strongest measures you can get, to crash this in- sorreetion, and don't let it spread." The other course Was to write to Austria and the other Powers of Europe, and impress upon them the necessity of not giving any assistance to these poor insurgents. (Shame.) Lord Derby said to the Turks" Arm your- selves, bring every force you can get to bear against these poor people, and stamp this insurrection out." To everybody else he said "I want fair play, we must not intervene, we must keep a ring," and he called it fair play to stand by and see a great strong empire of from twenty to thirty millions, drawing troops from Asia, from Egypt, as well as their European provinces, fighting against a poor, miserable, half-clad, half- starved, ntruegling peasant population. (Loud c, ies of" Shame.") He told them to crush the insurrec- tion, regardless of the consequences and cruel results, and he would stand by and keep everybody else from helping them. (A voice ; n That's Tory like, that is.") That was the key note of the whole of Lord Derby's policy almost up to the present , time. In diplomatic language' he deeired to maintain the status quo )f Turkey, and the integrity of the Turkish Em- pire ; and if lie h .d veered one iota from that policy, it was simply because he had been driven by the great gust of public feeling that had swept over the surface of the United Kingdom. (Loud cheers.) lie (Mr.ltylands) had no patience when he heard people speaking about theper- plexing problem of international polities. If a man dealt with them straightfordwardly, and in a proper spirit, there was no great perplexity in the problem to Ave. (Hear. hear.) We had certain leading prin- ciples, which might be traced in the history, and which lay at the root of the conscience of the Bntish people; and these leading principlea were the Inv° of freedom and justice to all the races of mankind. (Cheers.) It might be, when we saw a people struggling for free- dom, that we might not as a nation be in a position to render them efficient aid, but it was contrary to the feelings and principles of the British people thet.when 'La. nation was in the throes of such a struggle, to go in %Id oppose them, and prevent other nations from as- sisting them. (Loud cheers.) That was what we had done with the Turks, and we had supported that Power against a Christian people, who, although we were told they were little better than the Turks themselves, had even built schools, and taxed themselves for the education of their children, We were a Christian nation, professing to be in in favour of civil and religious liberty all over the woeld, and yet we had allowed our Government to take sides with, *Turkey against a Christian, an innocent, and Buffering people. That was contrary to British instincts, and BO long as we believed the wishes of the nation were not responded to we could not consent to give confi- dence to the British Government. He must say not only was the conduct of the Government such as to des- troy confidence, but he could see nothing in the recent speeches of members of the Government to inspire con- fidence in the future. (Hear, hear.) Lord Beacons- field—(hisses)—when speaking at a dinner in Bucking. bramshire had attempted to defend the policy of Her Majesty's Government. That was a most remarkable speech, and he was bound to notice it because in his judgment it was such as to excite amongst the people of this country a general feeling of considerable dissatis- faction and disappointment. Almost every passage in that speech contained a misrepresentation or an curacy. (Hear, hear.) Lord Beaeonsfield aid not seem even to have read the Blue Books, or if he had read them he made statements entirely at variance with the contents of the parliamentary papers laid on the tables of both Houses. There was also an element of defiance which seemed to show that he was prepared to neist the expression of public opinion in England, because he admitted that the public opinion was against the Government, and he had intimated plainly that he looked on that public opinion as a mere off- shoot of a large amount of ignorant enthusiasm, and therefore the Government were not prepared t 3 accept the public opinion of this cauntry as a guide for their pollee. He (Mr. Rylande) was not aware that there was any general opinion expressed by the people of this country which would be injurious to the interests of Great Britain or fatal to the peace of Europe. One of the matters which led to this imputation was the allegation that some leaders of the Liberal party had expressed an opinion that the Turks should he driven out of Europe. THE LII3ERAL LEGISLATION OF THE CENTURY. No. IT.° IN previous papers we have endeavoured to give a slight sketch of political feeling in this neighbourhood at the close of the last century; these were taken from the life of a Manchester Reformer. We now propose to carry the story forward to our own times, basing it for the most part, but not exclu- sively on the recollections of Lord Russell. We are not blind followers of that venerable statesman, and we shall not fail to indicate our points of difference; but we admire the consistency of a long life devoted to the ser- vice of his country; we are grateful for the influence of birth and education he has always brought to bear upon great prin- ciples; and if there have been some few aberrations, we gladly pass them over in the remembrance of good done in the past, and of the knowledge that the old statesman's heart—as witness his recent interest in the Servian cause—is yet true to the cause of liberty and progress. “Though old, he still retains His manly sense and energy of mind, Virtuous and wise he is, but not severe; He still remembers that he once was young." Lord Russell began his political life while he was still youthful. He was making an extended tour in Spain, where he learned to admire the calmness the directness, and the patriotism of the Duke of Wellington, when he received a letter from his father, the Duke of Bedford, to say that he was to be- come a candidate for Taviatock ; and he was elected one month before he came of age. He set forth in his political life with a light heart and full of hope, determined to do something worthy of his name, remember- ing his family motto—" Che sera sara,"— " What will be, will be." And now, at the close of sixty years' hard work, he says reverently, but possibly with the disappoint- ment we all feel when high hopes are merged into accomplished, but unsatisfactory reali- ties— sot heaven itself upon the past has power, What has been has been, and I have had my hour." Lord Russell was born in that stormy year of the French Revolution, 1792, when the valiant and patriotic Walker was getting into trouble for his Liberalism at Man- chester, We can fittingly take up the story from that date, and point out some of the very remarkable events whieh have occurred within the span of a single life. The nations of Europe were at peace, anti felt secure in the "balance of power." It was not merely that the physical forces of States were kept under a salutary restraint, but, as Miss Martineau so admirably points out, it was a much higher good that inter- national relations became more extended and refined : international morality was professed, and, to a certain degree, fostered: wild tempers and immediate objects were subdued and postponed to ulterior consider- ations: the weakest States became subjects of common protection, and the most outlying countries of general observation: the way was opened for commercial ,connections, and for mutual intercourses of every ameliorat- ing kind: and the States of Europe really appeared as securely settled in an advanced political civilisation as any nomad tribes who have entered upon the cultivation of land, and built themselves a town, and actually experienced that the blessings of social or- ganisation and impartial law are well worth the individual concessions by which they are purchased. The French Revolution, .with its horrors, disturbed this dream. Hitherto countries were parcelled out, bounded, and governed by diplomacy: it was a matter for statesmen only; but the time had come when the people asserted their right to be heard. During all this tumult abroad while em- peror and king were meeting at Pilnitz, and promising to assist their unhappy cousin in France, Pitt smiled calmly at the storm, and felt strong in his unassailable position. Parliament opened on the 31st January, 1792. The king's speech was one of con- gratulation and confidence. The aspect of Europe towards Great Britain was such that the king " was induced to think that some immediate reduction might safely be made in the naval and military establishments." There was congratulation also upon the" continual and. progressive improvement in the internal situation of the country." Everything looked like peace on- the side of France wrote Lord Granville, and although some in France wished for war her finances would not permit it. Congratula- tions did not end here. The King, when ad- dreeeing his "faithful commions " said—" I entertain the pleasing hope, that the reduc- tions which may be found practicable in the establishments, and the continued in- crease of the revenue, will enable you, after making due provision for the several branches of the public service, to enter upon' a system of gradually relieving my subjects from some part of the existing taxes, at the same time giving additional efficacy to the plfl fw the reduction of the national debt, on the 5uL"..."4 ei which our future ease and security essentially o."0";.°Eld." These are plain words, and however much we may ',.l..treCatt° part of Pitt's policy there is no &milt that he was sound in his principles of finance. In his celebrated Budget speech—to which we shall presently refer—he ascribed the merit of his scheme for the reduction of taxation, "in no small degree to the author of the 'Wealth of Nations,' an author now un- happily no more; whose existence and know- ledge of detail and depth of philosophical research will, I believe, furnish the best so- lution to eveiy question connected with the history of commerce or with the systems of political economy." The total revenue of the previous year was £16,730,000, out of this sum £lOO,OOO was paid to cancel exchequer bills, and £400,000 towards lessening the national debt. It was proposed to reduce the navy by 2,000 men, and to effect some retrenchment inthe army. The repeal of taxation proposed was :- 1, The last additional duty on malt £loo,ooo 2. Female servants -
3. A tax on wagons and carts £30,000 4. The three shilling house tax on houses with less than seven windows £56,000 5. The last halt-penny a pound on candles

Or a total of sss J • £220,000 He strongly advocated a reduction of the national debt, and thought the nation should change its rate of interest from 4 to 3 per cent. He looked for fifteen years of peace, and with it the consolidation of the Pountry whatever storms might rage abroad. We believe him to have been thoroughly honest and patriotic in all this; but alas for the vanity of human wisdom. Before the year was out the massacres of September at Paris had disgusted the English people,

and their warmest sympathisers could scarcely find apologies for their horrible brutality and coarseness. In December war was declared between the English and the French declared by the French who were flushed with their vic- tories. In the following January the na- tion was filled with horror when the News arrived of the minder of the French King, while at home, within a week of this event, the King in a message to Parliament stated the indispensable necessity of a fur- ther augmentation of forces by sea and land. Parliament responded to the call, and in an address to the throne, moved by Mr. Pitt, it was resolved "To offer to his Majesty our heartfelt condolence on the atrocious act lately perpetrated at Paris, which must be viewed by every nation in Europe as as out- rage on religion, justice, and humanity." It was further added—and the conduct of the French from their numerous and unexpected victories had made them so arrogant. we cannot wonder at the change ef feeling in England—" It is impossible for us not to be sensible of the views of aggrandizement and ambition, which, in violation of repeated and solemn professions, have openly been mani- fested on the part of France, and which are connected with the propagation of principles incompatible with the existence of all just and regular government: that under the present circumstances we consider a vigor- ous and effectual opposition to these views as essential to the security of everything which is most clear and valuable to us as a nation, and to the future tranquility and safety of all other countries." It was a sad anti-climax to the expressions of hope, and anticipations of happiness and prosperity n- dulged twelve months earlier. It was the beginning of a long bad time of retrogres- sion; but it was the natural reacti n from brutal excess. People were alarmed; Church and State, and royalty itself were supposed to be in danger, and capital, the I most timid of all things was imperilled. But we anticipate. There were good things pro- posed in 1792; proposals that were to lie dormant for a while, but that were to bear fruit by and by. Among these must be promi- nently mentioned Pitt's great speech against slavery. Some ten years prior to this time it had been asserted judicially in Westminster Hall that when once a negro touched the soil of England he was free. Numbers were able to claim their freedom, and it was natural—as we have recently witnessed it in America—that fierce contests of opini should arise between the advocates of slavery and of abolition. Many good men—like Newton, of Olney—adbered to the old form of things, but a school consisting of Zachary Macaulay, Granville Sharpe, Wilberforce. Henry Thornton, Clarkson, and others, rose up ; and being thoroughly convinced of the wickedness of slavery, as well as of its un- economical results, opposed it with all their power. Their efforts were so far successful , that they establ,shed a strong public opinion in favour of abolition, although emancipa- tion did. not follow for nearly forty years. On the 2nd April, 1792, there was a great debate in the Commons, in which both Fox , and Pitt spoke with rare eloquence. This speech is spoken of as one of Pitt's greatest efforts. He had compared the polish of old Rome with the barbarism of contemporary Britain; but we had long since emerged from this barbarism, though there still re- mained the disgrace of a barbarous traffic in slaves. "Sir," said he, " I trust we shall no loner continue this commerce, to the de• struction of every improvement on that wide continent (Africa) ; and shall not consider ourselves as conferring too great a boon in restoring its inhabitants to the rank of human beings. I trust we shall not think ourselves too liberal, if, by abolishing the slave trade, we give them the same comraon chance of civilisation with other parts of the world; and that we shall now allow to Africa the opportunity—the hope—the pro- spect of attaining to the same blessings which we ourselves, through the favourable dispensations of Divine Providence, have been permitted, at a much earlier period to enjoy. If we listen to the device of reason and duty, and pursue this night the line of conduct which they prescribe, some of us may live to see a reverse of that picture from which we now turn our eyes with shame and regret. We may live to behold the natives of Africa engaged in the calm occupations of industry, in the pursuits of a just anl legiti- mate commerce. We may behold the beams of science and philosophy breaking in upon their land, which, at some happy period in still later times, may blaze with full lustre, and joining their influence to that of pure reli- gion, may illuminate and invigorate the most distant extremeties of that immense continent. Then may we hope that even Africa, though last of all the quarters of the . globe, shall enjoy at length, in the evening of her days, those blessings which have de- scended so plentifully upon us in a much earlier period of the world. ihen also will Europe, participating in her improvement and prosperity, receive an ample recompense for the tardy kindness if kindness it can be called, of no longer hindering that continen. from extricating herself out of the darkness, which, in other more fortunate regions, has been so much more speedily dispelled. A CHEMICAL WORKS BURNT AT WIDNES, £20,000 DAMAGE. On Thmsday morring the extensive chemical works of the Widnes Alkali Company, Limited, were par- tially destroyed by fire, when a large amount of valu- able plant and stock was consumed, at an estimated loss of £20,000. Widnes is entirely dependent on its chemical manufactories, and the works belonging to this company employs over 500 men. About one o'clock smoke was obseived coming out of one of the sheds, and was rapidly followed by a large outburst of flame, the pitch pine and other combustible materials about the buildings giving every facility to the pro- gress of the Ore. The buzzer sounded the alarm, and in a few moments some thousands of persons assembled, but who appeared powerless to subdue the fury of the flames. Mr. C. E. Barlow, the secretory of the cora- pany, was at once sent for, and he, with other mem- bers of the company and officials of the firm, rendered what assistance was possible under the ercumstances. ! A note in pencil was sent to Hutchinson's works for their engine, but the person who received the note doubted its authenticity, and re quested to be supplied with a formal demand in writing before he could allow the engine to be despatched. All this caused delay, and misfortune seemed to attend every effort to obtain assistance. A messenger was also despatched to Warrington, but when the engine was got ready, strange to say, no horses could be procured, so the services of the Warrington brigade had to be dispensed with. In a very short time large portions of the salt cake and revolving sheds were in flames, all attempts to get the fire under being futile. In a large store- room, some 40 yards by 20 yards in extent, were stored about 800 tons of salt cake, worth a ton, and at two o'clock the iron flooring of the building gave way, the salt cake partially extinguishing the ilameo in thatpartionlar spot, and some huge iron columns in the,l fall partially demolishing two horizontal boilers. When the men saw that all attempts to save the ignited sheds wore hopeless they directed their attention to the ad- joining buildings, which cover an extensive area, with the idea of isolating as far as possible the remaining part of the plant. While they were making the attempt, the wind at this critical moment fortunately changed to an opposite direction, and thus prevented the entire destruction of the works. A new stern hoist was entirely destroyed, and two railway waggons were also partially consumed. Just before the fall of the salt carte shed two horses were rescued from the burning mass, and it is exceedingly fortunate consider- ing the great danger that attended the lire that no loss of life nor personal injury took place. The tire was not extinguished until it had spent its fury upon every. thing within its resell, and the ruin and desolation caused by the conflagration gives a faint idea of what a village is like when burnt by the Turks. Fortunately for the owners the loss is covered by insurance in the Royal Insurance Office, or during the present stagna- tion of the chemical trade the effect might have been felt to a serious degree by the company. Inspect°, Barnett, with a large stair of policemen, was in atten- dance, and energetically assisted to extinguish the fire, as did also Messrs. if. 8.
